Integrating anthropogenic hydrodynamics and GOCI satellite observations for water quality retrieval in highly engineered coastal systems: A case study of Saemangeum
Estimating hourly surface global and diffuse solar radiation across China using virtual radiation station networks
An improved GNSS-R ocean scatterometry recalibration approach using gradient boosting decision tree
abstract: Spaceborne Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) has developed rapidly for ocean scatterometry over the past three decades. However, residual signal calibration errors, arising from inaccuracies in some key parameters and the complex space environment, degrade its performance. In this work, we propose a one-step signal recalibration framework based on Gradient Boosting Decision Tree (GBDT) in a scaling correction manner guided by qualitative analyses. Results show good alignment between the learned and theoretical correction factors, wherein the bin ratio (BR) exhibits the dominant contribution. The recalibrated σ 0 exhibits lower sensitivity to calibration-related input features than the Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (CYGNSS) Version 2.1 (V2.1) σ 0 , and for several parameters, also lower sensitivity than the Version 3.2 (V3.2) σ 0 produced using traditional step-wise corrections during the period from January to June 2019. The maximum deviation of σ 0 across different wind speeds is also substantially reduced, leading to root mean square error (RMSE) of 1.52 m/s for ocean wind speed retrievals over 0–27 m/s, an improvement of 17.4% and 16.0% compared to using the V2.1 and V3.2 σ 0 products, respectively. Validation against buoy wind speed data shows an RMSE of 1.29 m/s and a bias of 0.020 m/s, representing reductions of 17.3% and 87.1%, respectively, relative to retrievals using the V3.2 σ 0 product. Feature importance analysis using SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) confirms consistency with theoretical expectations, especially regarding coupling effects between input features. The recalibrated σ 0 exhibits significantly reduced dependence on BR, GNSS-R satellites antennas, and Global Positioning System (GPS) transmitters, simultaneously. Furthermore, the spatial distribution of correction factors is strongly correlated with the noise floor, indicating that the proposed GBDT model identifies high-noise cases through BR and improves the robustness of σ 0 in these high-noise regions. As an alternative to step-wise empirical correction methods that could introduce artificial biases, the proposed recalibration method provides a new perspective and potential pathway for improving GNSS-R scatterometry.

title: NightFEST: A Feature-Enhanced SpatioTemporal fusion method for Nighttime light data from SDGSAT-1 GLI and NPP-VIIRS
RTAS: A radiative transfer model for agricultural strip-intercropping structures
Discrepancies between Sentinel-2 and LiDAR-derived LAI in temperate deciduous forests: Influence of apparent optical depth, radiative transfer priors, and horizontal heterogeneity
abstract: Accurate estimation of forests leaf area index (LAI) from satellite images remains challenging due to limited sunlight penetration and intricate scattering through structurally complex canopies. In this study, we compared LAI estimated from the inversion of the physical model PROSAIL applied to Sentinel2 (S2) images with LAI derived from airborne LiDAR scans across three temperate deciduous forests in France. We assessed three key factors to minimize discrepancies between both sources: (1) the optical signal attenuation caused by dense canopy, reducing the sensitivity of S2 reflectance to a limited canopy depth, (2) the impact of optimizing the parameterization of the PROSAIL inversion, and (3) the role of local horizontal heterogeneity in canopy height in driving residual errors. We found that S2 LAI estimates best matched LiDAR-derived LAI when the latter was restricted to the upper 48 m of canopy thickness. Optimizing PROSAIL parameters ranges reduced RMSE and bias, yet residual discrepancies remained largest in stands with strong horizontal heterogeneity within S2 pixels, where improvements in correlation and regression slope were limited. While the leaf mass area parameter configuration was robustly transferable across sites, other parameters (LAI, average leaf angle, brown pigments) required local tuning. These findings highlight the importance of accounting for canopy thickness and horizontal heterogeneity in canopy height when inferring LAI values from passive optical sensors, and suggest that future forest monitoring efforts using passive optical sensors may benefit from LiDAR-informed calibration strategies or hybrid inversion approaches that incorporate vertical and horizontal canopy information.

title: Improving regional winter wheat yield estimation by assimilating cross-scale heterogeneity information from UAV and satellite remote sensing
High-spatial-resolution mapping of annual anthropogenic heat flux in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei urban agglomeration using the CUNTLI-based inventory method
Tackling fluffy clouds: robust agricultural field boundary delineation from Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 satellite image time series
abstract: Accurate delineation of agricultural field boundaries is essential for effective crop monitoring and resource management. However, competing methodologies often face significant challenges, particularly in their reliance on extensive manual efforts for cloud-free data curation and limited adaptability to diverse global conditions. In this paper, we introduce PTAViT3D, a deep learning architecture specifically designed for processing three-dimensional time series of satellite imagery from either Sentinel-1 (S1) or Sentinel-2 (S2). Additionally, we present PTAViT3D-CA, an extension of the PTAViT3D model incorporating crossattention mechanisms to fuse S1 and S2 datasets, enhancing robustness in cloud-contaminated scenarios. The proposed methods leverage spatio-temporal correlations through a memory-efficient 3D Vision Transformer architecture, facilitating accurate boundary delineation directly from raw, cloud-contaminated imagery. We comprehensively validate our models through extensive testing on various datasets, including Australia’s ePaddocks™—CSIRO’s national agricultural field boundary product—alongside public benchmarks Fields-of-the-World, PASTIS, and AI4SmallFarms. Our results consistently demonstrate state-ofthe-art performance, highlighting excellent global transferability and robustness. Crucially, our approach significantly simplifies data preparation workflows by reliably processing cloud-affected imagery, thereby offering strong adaptability across diverse agricultural environments. Our code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/feevos/tfcl.

title: A scene-mapped framework for deriving clear-sky surface longwave downward radiation from remotely sensed measurements
Assessing plant area index and 3D plant area distribution in wheat canopies from a terrestrial LiDAR system for high-throughput plant phenotyping
abstract: This study investigates a new methodology to estimate plant area index ( PAI ) and its spatial distribution from 3D point clouds acquired by a system of 3 LiDARs (2 nadir-viewing and one at 45°) mounted on the Phenomobile Unmanned Ground Vehicle designed for high-throughput phenotyping of herbaceous crops. It relies on the computation of the gap fraction at the voxel level using the trajectories of the laser beams to numerically invert the Beer-Lambert law (BL), enabling the simultaneous estimation of PAI and AIA (Average Inclination Angle, in°). The method is evaluated on wheat crops both in silico (i.e. simulations based on the AdelWheat functional structural crop model coupled with a point cloud simulator) and in actual phenotyping trials of a panel of 10 bread wheat genotypes grown in two study sites under different treatments of plant density, water stress and sowing dates. The in silico validation indicates that the numeric inversion of BL with the LiDAR system of the Phenomobile leads to a relative error of 9.8% (RMSE = 0.32, R 2 = 0.99) and 8.4% (RMSE =5.4°, R 2 = 0.95) in the estimation of PAI and AIA , respectively. The validation in actual phenotyping experiments against destructive measurements produced satisfactory results for canopy PAI (RMSE = 1.44, R 2 = 0.82), while requiring prior knowledge on AIA , e.g. either by (i) introducing a regularization term in the cost function used to invert BL, to avoid unexpected high AIA estimations, (ii) using a fixed, reference value of 60°. The analysis of the results indicates that the inclusion of a regularization term mitigates the impact of actual differences in leaf inclination among cultivars on PAI accuracy, while providing a relative description of the actual variability in the vertical profile of leaf inclination across the different cultivars.

title: Towards continental-scale SWOT-based modeling of reservoir operations
abstract: The advent of reservoir models has enabled the monitoring and prediction of reservoir operations (inflow, storage, and release); however, the in situ operation data used for model parameterization is spatially scarce. In this study, we seek to expand global reservoir monitoring capabilities by leveraging observations from multiple satellite missions to reconstruct reservoir operation patterns, optimize reservoir model parameters, and simulate operations. We design a set of experiments relying on different combinations of in situ, satellite, and hydrologically modeled data sources as reservoir model inputs to characterize the error of satellite- and model-informed reservoir operations. We also make the first attempt to evaluate the use of the Surface Water and Ocean Topography (SWOT) satellite mission data record for reservoir optimization and simulation. Our results show that the accuracy of simulated releases is strongly dependent on the quality of the inflow time series. However, we find that integrating satellite-based (e.g., SWOT and other altimeters) reservoir operations with a hydrological model improves simulated release compared to naturalized flow alone, indicating that satellite- and model-derived inputs are useful for more accurately simulating human impacts on river systems. Given that SWOT has significantly greater spatial coverage of global reservoirs than previous satellite altimeters, our study advances the science of global reservoir monitoring using only remotely sensed and modeled data sources.

title: Estimation of rice leaf angle distribution from geometric features in millimetric-resolution UAV RGB imagery acquired at 45° viewing angle
abstract: Leaf angle distribution (LAD) is a fundamental determinant of canopy light interception and photosynthetic efficiency, yet its robust quantification remains a major bottleneck. Traditional methods are constrained by either labor-intensive manual measurements or the ill-posed nature of indirect gap probability inversion. Recent advances in deep learning have demonstrated great potential for directly extracting canopy traits from high-resolution imagery. However, whether 2D RGB imagery contains sufficient information to retrieve LAD, a three-dimensional canopy structural trait, is still questionable. We investigated this question by developing a deep learning framework that establishes the relationship between image-derived features and LAD from millimetric-resolution RGB images taken from a UAV. We focused on rice crops representing one of the main cultivated species. A total of 332 rice plants were digitized to construct realistic 3D canopies; we generated 21,600 paired images and GT LAD labels via physically based rendering. In silico experiments demonstrated that deep learning models enable efficient LAD estimation, particularly when taking images inclined at 45° perpendicularly to the rows. Further, our model achieved substantially higher accuracy for average inclination angle (AIA, R 2 = 0.608, RMSE = 1.590°) compared to gap probability-based inversion (R 2 = −0.788, RMSE = 3.397°). Finally, our model showed superior performance from the transplanting to booting stage (R 2 avg > 0.94 for LAD) when applied to actual observations. Application to over 1000 cultivars across two years confirmed high repeatability, establishing a scalable solution for large-scale monitoring. Interpretability analyses, supported by feature visualization and ablation studies, reveal that the model explicitly extracts geometric features specific to leaf inclination, while disentangling them from confounding canopy variables in millimetric-resolution RGB imagery. This feature-level discrimination underpins the model's superior accuracy and ensures robust generalization in diverse field scenarios.
